quiz.problem: This question has two defensible answers, and it copies the body's own example. Option b ("The tests should mock the database instead") is a real fix: a test fake is a second adapter, and the right option's own feedback recommends exactly that ("Add the seam when a second adapter, like an in-memory fake for tests, actually exists"). The setup (a store in front of Postgres, one adapter, tests on a real database) is lines 63 of the body almost word for word, so it tests recognition rather than transfer. Its "swap it later" premise also repeats Checkpoint real-seam's option b ("You might switch... one day").
quiz.evidence: Line 344: the feedback on [x] says to add the seam once an in-memory fake exists, which is what option b proposes. Line 63: "The comments module talks to the database directly, and only one adapter ever fills that slot: the real Postgres database. Even the tests use a real copy". Line 96: "You might switch to a different email provider one day."
quiz.fix:
Turn it around so it tests the same rule in a fresh setting (rename the id while it is still unpublished):
```test spot-removed-seam
Kai deletes the app's `PaymentGateway` interface, calling it "a pass-through". The live app plugged Stripe into it, and the tests plugged in a fake that records charges. Spot the mistake.
- [ ] His call was right: one function is too shallow to keep.
  > One function can hide a lot, and a seam is judged by what varies across it. Here two things did.
- [ ] It should have been renamed a boundary, since Stripe sits outside the app.
  > The vocabulary bans "boundary". The name was never the problem.
- [x] Two adapters filled it, so it was a real seam worth keeping.
  > Right. The real gateway and the test fake both plug in there. Without it, every test needs real Stripe.
- [ ] The deletion test backs him, because the live app still runs without it.
  > Look at every caller, tests included: each would now need real Stripe or its own workaround. The complexity comes back, so it was earning its keep.
```
If you would rather keep a one-adapter question, move it to a fresh setting (for example a `SettingsSource` around a settings file, "in case we move to a settings server", with tests reading a real sample file). Then replace option b with "Settings code is too small to be a module at all." and this feedback: "A module can be any size, even one function. Size isn't the issue."

Ana's survey report has four cards, every one badged `Speculative`. Feeling the run must produce something, she turns all four into tickets. What's the mistake?

quiz.problem: The prompt restates the right answer's defining phrase. "I fixed the rounding bug once, and every page... got the fix" is the highlighted line 39 "fix it once, fixed everywhere", so this is recognition. The framing also leans on many callers ("every page that shows a price"), which is how the Skill defines leverage ("One implementation pays back across N call sites"). That is why option b's feedback has to open with "Close, but". Option d (shallowness because the fix was small) isn't a real misconception.
quiz.evidence: Line 39: "==fix it once, fixed everywhere==". Line 398: the prompt. Line 402: "Close, but leverage is what callers get". codebase-design SKILL.md: "Leverage... One implementation pays back across N call sites and M tests."
quiz.fix:
```test why-locality
Before a deepening, fixing a rounding bug meant hunting through five files that each rounded prices their own way. Now there's one place to look and one place to change. Which benefit of depth is that?
- [x] Locality, which maintainers get
  > Right. Change, bugs and checking now live in one place, so a fix there is a fix everywhere.
- [ ] Leverage, which callers get
  > Leverage is what callers get: more capability per thing they learn. This is about where a maintainer has to look and change.
- [ ] A real seam, since prices now pass through one spot
  > A seam is where adapters can be swapped. Nothing is being swapped here.
- [ ] Depth in the implementation, since the module now holds more code
  > Depth is measured at the interface, not by how much code sits inside. What the maintainer feels here is locality.
```

quiz.problem: This is recall, not transfer. The prompt asks what "Matt's docs suggest", and the right answer restates line 176 almost word for word ("pointing it at the spec and asking 'how can we make this change easy?'"). A reader can match the sentence without understanding why a direction matters (hot-spot scoping).
quiz.evidence: Line 176: "Before a big build, Matt's docs suggest pointing it at the spec (the written plan) and asking 'how can we make this change easy?'" Line 303: "Point it at the spec and ask how to make that change easy."
quiz.fix:
Ask about the consequence instead. The right answer stays in position a:
```test scenario-big-build
Next week you build a large feature from a finished spec. It reworks the checkout code, which nobody has touched in a year. Today you type `/improve-codebase-architecture` with nothing after it. What's the risk?
- [x] It follows recent changes, so it may never look at checkout.
  > Right. With no direction it follows the hot spots in the history. Point it at the spec and ask how to make that change easy.
- [ ] It will start refactoring the checkout code before you're ready.
  > It never changes code. The risk is where it looks, not what it edits.
- [ ] With no direction it won't run until you name a module.
  > It doesn't need one: it infers hot spots from the history. That's exactly why it may miss checkout.
- [ ] It skips `GLOSSARY.md` and the ADRs when no direction is given.
  > It reads the project's words and decisions either way. The problem is the scope it picks.
```
